title: Who made the rubber boom possible?
essentialQuestion: Who gained from rubber in British Malaya and Singapore, who did the work, and what can an old picture not tell us?
learningGoal: Explain who gained and who worked in the rubber boom, using two sources, and say what a 1914 picture of rubber tapping cannot show.

warmUp.question: Think of one car tyre. How many people do you think worked to make it?

evidence.question: Which source tells you about owners and investors? Which tells you about workers? What does the picture show?

sources.caption: Source 1: “From Gambier to Pepper: Plantation Agriculture in Singapore”, by Timothy Pwee (National Library Board Singapore, 2021)
details: A modern history article in the library's magazine, BiblioAsia.
It says cars and electricity made people want rubber, for tyres and for covering electric wires.
It says the merchant Tan Chay Yan started Asahan Estate in Melaka in 1898, and Chinese merchants later set up rubber companies in Singapore.
It says London companies bought many estates. One group held more than 12,000 acres in Singapore by 1912.
Limit: it shows possible profit for owners and investors. It says almost nothing about workers' pay.

sources.caption: Source 2: “Indian Migration into Malaya and Singapore During the British Period”, by Makeswary Periasamy (National Library Board Singapore, 2007)
details: A modern history article in BiblioAsia.
It says most Indian workers came from South India under indenture or the kangany system, and a few came as free workers.
Indentured workers were tied to one employer for some years. Many had debts, and their pay was lower than free workers' pay. Indenture ended in 1910.
Under the kangany system, an overseer recruited workers, and more families came. Critics said it misled some people. It ended in 1938.
Limit: it describes systems and what happened to some workers. It is not one worker's own story.

sources.caption: Source 3: A photo of rubber tapping in the book Souvenir of Singapore, 1914
details: Printed in 1914 in a souvenir book published by a Singapore hotel, the Grand Hotel de l'Europe. The photographer is not known.
It shows rows of rubber trees, a worker at a tree trunk with a bucket, and a second worker further back.
Limit: it cannot show the workers' names, pay, contracts or feelings. The book's makers chose this scene for a souvenir.

events.text: Tan Chay Yan starts Asahan Estate, a rubber estate in Melaka.
Indenture for Indian workers ends. Chinese merchants set up rubber companies in Singapore.
One group of London companies holds more than 12,000 acres of land in Singapore.
Souvenir of Singapore prints a photo of rubber tapping (Source 3).
Recruitment of workers through the kangany system ends.

sections.heading: Why people wanted rubber
sections.text: Around 1900, more people began to use cars and electricity. Car tyres were made with rubber, and electric wires needed a rubber cover to keep them safe. So people wanted much more rubber. In British Malaya and Singapore, land was cleared and rubber trees were planted. A rubber tree gives a milky liquid called latex. A worker tapped each tree by cutting a thin line in its bark, carefully, so the tree was not harmed. Then workers collected the latex, and others made it into flat sheets that could be shipped. Rubber grew on large estates and on small farms too.
sections.simpler: Around 1900, people began to use cars and electricity. Car tyres needed rubber. Electric wires needed a rubber cover. So people wanted lots of rubber. In Malaya and Singapore, people planted rubber trees. A rubber tree gives a white liquid called latex. A worker cuts a thin line in the tree. Workers collect the latex. Then it is made into sheets and sent away. Rubber grew on big estates and on small farms.

sections.heading: Owners, investors and workers
sections.text: Rubber could bring big profits, but starting an estate cost a lot of money. In 1898, a merchant called Tan Chay Yan started Asahan Estate in Melaka, one of the first in Malaya. Later, an investor in London could buy shares in a company that owned estates. Many workers came from South India. Some came under indenture, a contract that tied a worker to one employer for several years. Many indentured workers had debts, and their pay was lower than that of free workers. Indenture ended in 1910. Under the kangany system, an overseer recruited workers, and more families came. Some people came freely. These systems help explain why a worker's choices were not the same as an owner's.
sections.simpler: Rubber could make owners rich. In 1898, a merchant called Tan Chay Yan started a rubber estate. Later, an investor in London could pay money into rubber companies. Many workers came from South India. Some came under indenture. This contract tied them to one boss for years. Many had debts and low pay. Indenture ended in 1910. In the kangany system, a boss found workers. More families came this way. Some people came freely.

sections.heading: What a souvenir picture shows
sections.text: The second picture is a photo printed in 1914 in a souvenir book about Singapore. A Singapore hotel published the book as a souvenir. The photo shows rows of rubber trees and a worker at a tree with a bucket. The book's makers chose this scene to show visitors. The photo cannot tell us the workers' names or pay. It cannot tell us how they came, or whether they were free to leave. For those questions, we need other sources, such as pay records, contracts or a worker's own account. One photo from Singapore also cannot stand for every estate in Malaya.
sections.simpler: The second picture is a photo from 1914. It is in a book for visitors to Singapore. It shows rubber trees. A worker sits at a tree with a bucket. The book chose this scene. The photo does not tell us the name or pay of the worker. It does not tell us if they were free to leave. For that, we need other sources, like pay records or the words of workers.

glossary.definition: The white liquid that comes out of a cut rubber tree.
glossary.example: Workers collected the latex in small cups and buckets.

glossary.definition: A very large farm where one crop is grown to sell.
glossary.example: Tan Chay Yan started a rubber estate in Melaka in 1898.

glossary.definition: Someone who puts money into a business, hoping to get more back.
glossary.example: An investor in London could own part of a rubber estate in Malaya.

glossary.definition: A work contract that tied a worker to one employer for years.
glossary.example: Indenture for Indian workers in Malaya ended in 1910.

glossary.definition: A way of finding workers through a work boss, or overseer.
glossary.example: Under the kangany system, more families came to work on estates.

checks.question: Why did people want much more rubber around 1900?

options.text: For car tyres and for covering electric wires
options.feedback: Yes. More people used cars and electricity, and both needed rubber.

options.text: For building new houses and roads
options.feedback: Not quite. Look at the first part of the reading. Which two new things needed rubber?

options.text: For making paper and printing books
options.feedback: Not quite. The first part of the reading names two uses. Read it again.

checks.question: Can the 1914 photo show how much a rubber tapper was paid?

options.text: Yes, because the bucket shows how much they earned
options.feedback: Not quite. A bucket shows the work, not the pay. Read the third part again.

options.text: No, we need a pay record or a worker's own account
options.feedback: Yes. A photo shows what the camera saw. Pay is written in records, or told by the worker.

options.text: Yes, because it was printed in a book
options.feedback: Not quite. Being in a book does not show pay. Look at what the third part says we need.

write.prompt: Make a table with three rows. Write one gain and who got it. Write one cost for workers. Write one question the sources cannot answer.
sentenceStarters: One benefit was ..., and it went to ...
The source that shows this is ...
One cost or limit for some workers was ...
One question the sources cannot answer is ...
selfCheck: I named one benefit and who got it.
I named one cost or limit for workers, with a source.
I wrote one question the sources cannot answer.
write.example: One benefit was money from selling rubber. It went to owners and investors. The 2021 library article shows this. It says Tan Chay Yan started an estate, and London companies bought big estates. One cost for some workers was indenture. It tied them to one boss for years, and many had debts and low pay. One question the sources cannot answer is how much the worker in the 1914 photo was paid.

speak.partnerTask: With a partner, trace the latex from the tree to a buyer far away. Name one person's work at each step. Then name one voice the sources are missing.
speak.independentTask: Draw or write the four steps from tree to buyer. Next to each step, write whose work it needed. Circle one voice that is missing.

reflect.completionMessage: You finished Lesson 5. You used sources to show who gained from rubber and who did the work.

visual.description: PLACEHOLDER: not drawn yet. An original Thinkerwell diagram of a simple chain of four boxes from left to right, joined by arrows, headed "From tree to buyer" with the label "simplified: not the only way the business worked". Box 1 "Tree and tapper": a rubber tree with a thin cut line and a small cup, and a plain figure tapping it (no face details, no costume). Box 2 "Processing": a plain figure pressing latex into flat sheets. Box 3 "Shipping": a plain figure carrying a bundle of sheets towards a simple ship at a dock. Box 4 "Buyer far away": a car tyre and a coil of covered wire. Above the chain, a separate box "Owners and investors" with a dashed line to the word "profit". Below the chain, one callout "Who earned? Who worked?". No flags, no real company names, no real people. Words carry every meaning; colour is never the only clue.
visual.alt: A chain of four steps from a rubber tree to a buyer: a worker taps the tree, a worker makes the latex into sheets, a worker carries the sheets to a ship, and a buyer far away uses the rubber for tyres and wires. Above the chain, owners and investors are linked to profit. A callout asks: Who earned? Who worked?
visual.caption: A simple Thinkerwell diagram of how rubber got from a tree to a buyer. Real farms and companies worked in many ways.
visual.lookClosely: Which steps would a photo of a rubber estate leave out?

secondVisual.description: Wikimedia Commons file "Souvenir of Singapore, 1914 - Plate 10 - Rubber Tapping.jpg": plate 10 of the book Souvenir of Singapore, 1914 (Singapore: Grand Hotel de l'Europe), photographer unknown. A black-and-white photo of rows of thin rubber trees with dry leaves on the ground; one worker crouches at a trunk with a bucket beside them, and a second worker crouches further back. Chosen because it is a dated, published image that shows the work clearly but was made for visitors, which lets learners separate what a picture shows from pay, contracts and choices it cannot show.
secondVisual.alt: A black-and-white photo of rows of thin rubber trees, with dry leaves covering the ground. A worker crouches close to a tree trunk, working on the bark, with a bucket beside them. A second worker crouches near a tree further back.
secondVisual.caption: A photo of rubber tapping printed in a Singapore souvenir book in 1914. It records what the book chose to show, not the workers' pay or views.
secondVisual.lookClosely: What work can you see? What would a pay record add?

sensitiveNotes: Indenture and kangany recruitment meant debt, hard work and low pay for many workers; the National Library article says critics called indenture “near slavery” and said kangany recruiters misled some people. Keep both truths: don't call every migrant enslaved, and don't call every arrangement free. Some learners may have moved for work, or know people who did: never ask learners about their own or their family's journeys, work, pay, legal status, home country, religion or ethnicity. There is no worker's own account in this lesson, and none should be invented; when learners imagine a worker, they write questions to investigate, not a made-up life story.
educatorNotes: Aim: learners back one benefit and one worker constraint with a source, and say what the 1914 photo cannot show. Evidence move (brief 3B): pair the investor record (Source 1) with the recruitment history (Source 2), then look at the 1914 souvenir photo. A sound answer gives a benefit and a constraint backed by sources, not guessed from the picture. Misconceptions to catch: not every Indian migrant was a rubber tapper (many were merchants, clerks or teachers), not every tapper was indentured, ownership was not only British (Tan Chay Yan and other Chinese merchants owned estates, and small farmers grew rubber), and one Singapore photo cannot stand for every estate in Malaya.

Source caveats: both National Library articles are modern histories, not workers' records. The 12,000 acres belonged to one group of London companies, not to all rubber land. The 1914 book was made by a hotel for its guests. The National Heritage Board's record for a similar postcard says indenture tied workers to a three-year contract; the National Library article says five years at first, cut to three in 1872, so the lesson says “several years”.
changes: Written on 1 November 2026 from Justin's course brief (28 October 2026), sections 3 and 3A.

Facts checked against both National Library Board articles and the National Heritage Board record, opened on 1 November 2026. 3A says the kangany system “ended as an assisted-emigration system in 1938”; the article says it was abolished in 1938 when India banned all assisted emigration, so the timeline says recruitment through it ended in 1938.

3A's “London companies later bought large plantation holdings, sometimes giving local owners shares” is simplified in the reading to investors buying shares; the detail stays in Source 1. The reading does not say rubber was the only crop or that Malaya's workers were all Indian.

Commons file checked on 1 November 2026: author unknown, about 1914, from Souvenir of Singapore, 1914 (Grand Hotel de l'Europe, Singapore, via the National Library's e-books), public domain in Singapore (PD-SG-photo) and the United States (PD-1923), as the brief says. The brief did not name the publisher; it is a hotel, which the lesson uses as evidence of the book's purpose. Alt text written from the image itself.
The Read part 1 line about the bark is based on the National Library article's note that Ridley's tapping method let trees be tapped regularly without harm.
